question: Heart surgeons were tracked through years of a new operation. Whose failed operations most improved their later results?
answer: Colleagues' failures. KC, Staats and Gino found surgeons improved after their own successes and after colleagues' failures, but not after their own failures. A failure of one's own was easier to blame on bad luck or a hard patient; someone else's was looked at plainly.
move: Study your own failures as coldly as you would study someone else's.
ask: Which of my own mistakes have I explained away that I would call a lesson if a friend had made it?
trap: A painful mistake of one's own seems the best teacher.
source: KC, Staats and Gino, Management Science, 2013
reference: KC, Staats and Gino, Learning from My Success and from Others' Failure: Evidence from Minimally Invasive Cardiac Surgery, Management Science, 2013
